title: Snapshot state & recomposition
scopeHtml: Scope: State/MutableState, the snapshot system (isolation, observers, apply, conflicts), recomposition scopes and skipping, observable collections, background-thread writes, backwards writes and recomposition ordering. Stability rules are in the stability chunk; remember/derivedStateOf/hoisting are in the remember chunk; effects are in the effects chunk.

questions.promptHtml: What is State<T> in Compose, what does mutableStateOf give you, and what exactly makes a composable recompose when the value changes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who memorized by remember { mutableStateOf() } from people who know recomposition is driven by reads of observable objects, not by "the variable changed".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "State<T> is a read-only observable holder; MutableState<T> adds a setter. mutableStateOf creates a snapshot-aware object. When composable code reads .value, the runtime records 'this recompose scope read this state'. When the value is written and the change is applied, every scope that read it is invalidated and re-executed on the next frame. No read, no recomposition. A plain var is invisible to Compose."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
MutableState<T> is an interface with var value: T. The implementation (SnapshotMutableStateImpl) is a StateObject: it keeps a linked list of versioned records, one per snapshot that wrote to it. Reading .value calls readable(...), which (1) picks the record visible to the current snapshot and (2) notifies the current snapshot's read observer. During composition, that observer is installed by the Composer for the current recompose scope. Writing .value calls overwritable(...); if the new value is equivalent (default policy: structural ==) to the old one, nothing happens. Otherwise a new record is created and, once the snapshot is applied, apply observers fire and the Recomposer invalidates scopes that had read this object.

 read in composition                write (event handler / coroutine)
 Text(count)  --reads--> [State] <--writes-- onClick { count++ }
      |  read observer records (scope -> state)
      v
 state changed + snapshot applied -> Recomposer invalidates the scope -> next frame re-runs it

Three declaration styles are equivalent (val s = remember { mutableStateOf(0) }, var v by remember { ... } with getValue/setValue imports, and destructuring val (v, setV)). State<T> as a type matters in APIs: it signals "you may read, you may not write", and passing State<T> instead of T lets a child read it lazily (see Q042).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Counter() {
    var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }   // observable, survives recomposition
    var broken = 0                                // plain local: reset every recomposition, not observed
    Button(onClick = { count++; broken++ }) {
        Text("count=$count broken=$broken")       // broken always shows 0 (or 1 transiently)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting remember: a new MutableState is created every recomposition, so the value resets and nothing sticks.
  • Believing mutableStateOf survives configuration change. It does not; that is rememberSaveable.
  • Thinking recomposition re-runs the parent. Only scopes that read the state re-run.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does writing the same value trigger recomposition? → No for the default structural policy: equivalent(old, new) is true so no new record is written.
  2. Is State<T> thread-safe? → Reads/writes are snapshot-safe; the read-modify-write x.value += 1 is not atomic across threads (see Q031).
  3. What if the state is read in a lambda that runs later (onClick)? → That read is not inside composition, so it subscribes nothing; it just reads the current value.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "state change triggers recomposition." Senior: describes read tracking, the record list, equivalence policies, and that a write is not "seen" until the snapshot is applied.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team stored a feature flag in a plain var inside a holder class; the UI updated only when something else happened to recompose. Moving it to mutableStateOf fixed the "toggle needs two taps" bug.

questions.promptHtml: What is a recompose scope? If a Text deep inside a Column reads a state, what actually re-executes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates often say "the whole screen recomposes". The senior answer knows the unit of invalidation and why Column/Row/Box don't count.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The unit of recomposition is the nearest enclosing restartable composable function, or composable lambda, that read the state. The compiler wraps each such function body in a RecomposeScope. Inline composables like Column, Row, Box don't create their own scope, so a read inside their content lambda invalidates the enclosing function. Only that function re-runs, then its callees are skipped if their inputs are unchanged."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The compiler transforms each non-inline @Composable returning Unit into code that calls composer.startRestartGroup(key) / endRestartGroup()?.updateScope { ... }. The returned ScopeUpdateScope lets the runtime re-invoke that exact function with its last parameters. State reads register against whichever scope is current.

@Composable fun Screen() {            <- scope A
    Column {                          <- inline: part of A
        Header(title)                 <- scope B (skippable if title unchanged)
        Text("Count: ${count}")       <- Text is non-inline but read happens in A's lambda body
    }                                 <-  string template evaluated in A  => A invalidated
}

The subtle point: "Count: ${count}" is evaluated as an argument in Screen's body, so Screen's scope reads count, not Text's. Text receives a new String and recomposes because its parameter changed. To narrow the read, push it into a smaller composable (CountText()), or pass a lambda () -> Int. Lambdas passed to non-inline composables (e.g. content of a custom Card) get their own scope.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Screen(vm: CounterVm) {
    val count by vm.count.collectAsState()   // read of this State happens below, where `count` is used
    Column {
        Header()                              // skipped: no params changed
        Text("Count: $count")                 // `count` read in Screen's scope -> Screen re-runs
    }
}
// Narrower: read inside its own function so only CountText re-runs
@Composable fun CountText(count: State<Int>) { Text("Count: ${count.value}") }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming every composable is a boundary. inline ones aren't, and non-restartable ones (@NonRestartableComposable, non-Unit return) aren't either.
  • Reading state in the parent "just to pass it down", which invalidates the parent.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Column not create a scope? → It is inline; its content lambda is inlined into the caller.
  2. How do you see the scopes? → Layout Inspector recomposition counts (and compiler reports show restartable/skippable).
  3. Does a non-skippable scope still limit work? → Yes: it re-runs its own body, but children are still skipped individually if they are skippable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "only the composables using the state recompose." Senior: names the restart group, identifies where the read actually occurs textually, and fixes it by moving the read.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "typing indicator" boolean read at the top of a chat screen recomposed the header, the list adapter code and the input bar for every toggle. Moving the read into the one composable that needed it dropped recompositions by orders of magnitude (measured with Layout Inspector counts).

questions.promptHtml: When does Compose skip a composable during recomposition, and when can't it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Skipping is the mechanism that makes recomposition cheap. Interviewers want the real eligibility rules, not "if nothing changed".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "During recomposition the parent re-calls the child. If the child is skippable and every parameter compares equal to last time, the compiler-generated code skips the body. By the official docs a function is not skippable if it has a non-Unit return type, is annotated @NonRestartableComposable or @NonSkippableComposable, or has a non-stable parameter. Strong skipping mode relaxes the stability requirement."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The compiler adds a $changed int bitmask parameter per composable. For stable params, it compares the new value to the slot-table-stored previous value with equals; for unstable params in classic mode it treats them as always changed. If all bits say "same" and no read state invalidated this scope, it calls composer.skipToGroupEnd().

Parameter type Classic (pre strong skipping) Strong skipping on
Primitive / String / lambda Stable, equals Same
@Stable/@Immutable class equals Same
Unstable class (e.g. List<T>, class with var) Always "changed", never skipped Compared by instance (===)

Strong skipping became the default with Kotlin 2.0.20 (compiler plugin shipped with Kotlin; it was experimental from Compose compiler 1.5.4). Verify for your exact toolchain via compiler reports. Important: skipping is only an optimization. Correctness must not depend on a composable running or not running.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Row1(title: String, onClick: () -> Unit) { /* skippable if title equals and lambda equal/remembered */ }

@Composable
fun Price(): Int = 5   // returns non-Unit: not skippable, not restartable

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Compose skips if the data is equal": not if the type is unstable in classic mode.
  • Believing a skipped composable can never show new data: it can if it reads State internally, since that invalidates its own scope.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is List<String> unstable? → List is an interface that may be backed by a MutableList; the compiler cannot prove immutability (details in the stability section).
  2. If a scope is skipped, are its children skipped? → Yes; nothing in it runs.
  3. What if only a State read inside the child changed? → The child's own scope is invalidated and re-run even though its params are equal.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "if parameters are the same it skips." Senior: lists exclusions, knows $changed and strong skipping, and treats skipping as an optimization not a contract.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a Kotlin upgrade enabled strong skipping, a screen that relied on a new List instance each time to force refresh stopped updating, because the new-but-equal list compared equal. See the post-upgrade regression scenarios elsewhere in this bank.

questions.contextHtml:
A junior's shopping-cart screen. Product: 300k DAU. QA report: "Tapping Add shows the item only after rotating the phone." Code:

@Composable
fun CartScreen() {
    val items = remember { mutableStateOf(mutableListOf<CartItem>()) }
    Column {
        items.value.forEach { CartRow(it) }
        Button(onClick = { items.value.add(CartItem("sku-${items.value.size}")) }) { Text("Add") }
    }
}

Logs show add executes (size grows). Red herring: the dev suspects the Button ripple/interaction state.
questions.promptHtml: Why does the UI not update, and how would you fix it in two ways?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap in remember" (already there) or "call notifyDataSetChanged-like invalidation". Doesn't know the state object holds a reference and add never writes to the state.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the list reappear after rotation (then the data is changing, it's the notification)? Is the same CartItem type stable/immutable? Is this state meant to survive rotation? Who else mutates the list?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; swap to an observable collection.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) mutation of a non-observable collection inside state, the MutableState was never written; (b) item key issue; (c) button not receiving clicks; (d) recomposition suppressed by an unstable param. Only (a) fits "appears after rotation" because rotation recreates the composition and re-reads the list.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add a log line when items.value is read. Layout Inspector recomposition count stays 0 on tap. Debug items.value.size after tap.
  5. Root cause: items.value.add(...) mutates the list object. The MutableState.value setter is never called, so no state record is written, no apply observer fires, the scope is never invalidated.
  6. Fix: Either val items = remember { mutableStateListOf<CartItem>() } and items.add(...), which is itself snapshot-aware and notifies on add, or hold an immutable List in state and replace it: items.value = items.value + newItem. Prefer immutable replacement when the list is exposed from a ViewModel as StateFlow<List<...>>.
  7. Prevention: Lint/review rule: no mutableListOf/ArrayList inside mutableStateOf; rememberSaveable needs a Saver for a state list.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't force recomposition by neverEqualPolicy + reassigning the same list; it works but hides the model problem and defeats equality checks.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if you used remember { mutableStateListOf<CartItem>() } and the screen rotates? → The list is lost because remember doesn't survive; use rememberSaveable with a Saver or hoist into a ViewModel.
  • Would items.value = items.value fix the original? → Not with the default policy: same reference is structurally equal, so no change. neverEqualPolicy would.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from several teams: a settings screen kept a MutableMap inside a State and "worked" in debug because the debugger's tap handling happened to recompose the screen via an unrelated animation. In release the animation was gone and the bug appeared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Cannot explain why the UI does not update; suggests calling invalidate.
  • Hire: Identifies non-observable mutation; fixes with mutableStateListOf or immutable copy.
  • Strong hire: Explains the write path (no record, no apply notification), the neverEqualPolicy trap, and how to choose between the two fixes for ViewModel exposure.

questions.promptHtml: How do mutableStateListOf and mutableStateMapOf differ from mutableStateOf(listOf(...)), and what are the traps when using them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you understand granularity of observation and the hidden cost/semantics of snapshot-aware collections.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "SnapshotStateList and SnapshotStateMap are mutable collections that are themselves snapshot state: structural changes (add, remove, set) are tracked, and any scope that read the list (iteration, size, get) is invalidated. With mutableStateOf(listOf()) I replace the whole list and invalidate on every replacement, comparing by equals. The observable collections give in-place updates, but they observe at collection level, not per element, so one set(i, x) still invalidates every scope that read the list."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SnapshotStateList is a StateObject whose current record holds a persistent (copy-on-write) list internally (verify the exact structure: it is not exposed API). A write creates a new record for the writing snapshot, so a recomposition reading in one snapshot never sees half-applied changes, and ConcurrentModificationException is not thrown for cross-snapshot reads. Two ways to read cheaply: read through get(index)/size only where needed; use LazyColumn(items = list) which reads in the lazy list's scope.

mutableStateOf(List) mutableStateListOf
Update Replace reference (O(n) copy on add) In place (internally persistent, amortized)
Equality check on set equals on the full list none (structural change tracked by modCount)
Fine-grained per element? No No
Exposed to UI as List<T> (unstable in classic mode) SnapshotStateList<T> (stable by compiler special-casing; verify)
Save across rotation rememberSaveable with Saver rememberSaveable with Saver (toMutableStateList())

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val tags = remember { mutableStateListOf("a", "b") }
tags += "c"            // observable
tags[0] = "z"          // observable
// Per-item observation requires per-item state:
class Row(val id: Long, initial: Boolean) { var checked by mutableStateOf(initial) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting item-level invalidation; only a per-item MutableState gives that.
  • Sorting via list.sortBy {} in composition: it writes during composition (see Q034).
  • Exposing the mutable collection from a ViewModel; UI code can mutate it from anywhere.
  • Mutating the same SnapshotStateList from multiple threads without a snapshot; each op is atomic-ish but compound ops (check then add) are not.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you get a stable immutable read? → Expose List<T> (or ImmutableList) built from toList().
  2. Can you use mutableStateListOf in a ViewModel? → Possible, but I prefer a StateFlow<UiState> for testability; see the state holder section.
  3. Why is list[i] = x not enough for per-row updates in a LazyColumn? → It invalidates scopes that read the list, then every row whose params changed (and unstable params in classic mode) recompose; keys and stable rows limit that.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use mutableStateListOf so the UI updates." Senior: contrasts granularity and copy cost, calls out threading and saveability, and knows per-item state is the true fine-grain tool.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed with a mutableStateListOf of 2,000 items updated 5 times per second from a websocket recomposed visible rows on each insert until items were keyed and the batching described in Q039 was added.

questions.promptHtml: What is a SnapshotMutationPolicy, what are the three built-ins, and when would you change the default?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It reveals whether you know the equality check happens at write time and that mutableStateOf has a pluggable "did it change" rule.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A policy decides whether a write counts as a change (equivalent) and how to merge concurrent changes from different snapshots (merge). The default is structuralEqualityPolicy, using ==. referentialEqualityPolicy uses ===. neverEqualPolicy treats every write as a change, which is the escape hatch for mutating an object in place and still forcing notification."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: On state.value = new, the runtime calls policy.equivalent(current, new). If true, the write is dropped and nothing is invalidated. This is why setting an equal data class does nothing, even though it is a different instance. Referential policy is useful when equals is expensive or deliberately lies (huge lists, bitmaps). neverEqualPolicy is used by MutableStateFlow-less event holders and when wrapping legacy mutable models: val state = mutableStateOf(model, neverEqualPolicy()) then state.value = model after mutation. It also makes all concurrent writes conflict because equivalent is never true and merge returns null (the default merge), which matters for Q033. compositionLocalOf and derivedStateOf also accept policies.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val a = mutableStateOf(User("x"))                       // structural: == on data class
val b = mutableStateOf(bigImmutableTree, referentialEqualityPolicy())
val c = mutableStateOf(legacyModel, neverEqualPolicy())
legacyModel.name = "y"; c.value = legacyModel           // forces notification

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• neverEqualPolicy as a general fix for "UI not updating"; it also triggers recomposition for identical writes, creating loops if written in composition.
  • Using structural policy on huge collections: == is O(n) on every write.
  • Custom policy whose equivalent isn't symmetric/transitive.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the default merge do? → Returns null, so concurrent conflicting writes fail to apply.
  2. Do derivedStateOf results use a policy? → Yes (policy parameter, default structural).
  3. Referential policy and data class copy with equal content? → Treated as a change, recomposes consumers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: knows equal values don't recompose. Senior: ties the policy to write-time filtering, merge, and chooses referential for large immutable graphs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard stored a 5,000-point chart model in state with structural equality; each emission ran a deep equals on the main thread (about 6 ms). Switching to referential policy plus emitting new instances only when data changed removed it.

questions.promptHtml: Explain Compose's snapshot system. What problem does it solve, and what are the global snapshot and a mutable snapshot?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The snapshot system is the real engine under mutableStateOf. Knowing it separates users of Compose from people who can debug it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A snapshot is an isolated, consistent view of all state objects at a point in time, like MVCC in a database. Reads inside a snapshot see the values as of its creation plus its own writes. A mutable snapshot's writes stay invisible to everyone else until apply() publishes them atomically, or are discarded on dispose. There's always a global snapshot that holds 'real' state. Composition runs inside a mutable snapshot, so composables never see half-applied writes from other threads."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each StateObject keeps a linked list of StateRecords tagged with the snapshot id that wrote them. A snapshot has an id and a set of invalid ids (snapshots opened after it, or not yet applied). Reading picks the newest record whose id is valid for the reading snapshot. Writing in a snapshot either reuses a record the snapshot already owns or copies the current one into a new record.

 Global snapshot (id 10)  --- state X: rec(id=10, value=1)
        |
   takeMutableSnapshot()  -> S (id 11)
   S.enter { X.value = 2 }  -> X gets rec(id=11, value=2); global still sees 1
   S.apply()                -> X's record 11 becomes valid for global; apply observers fire
   S.dispose()              -> frees bookkeeping; undisposed snapshots keep old records alive (leak)

From the official docs: a mutable snapshot's changes are atomic ("all or none"); Snapshot.enter makes it the thread's current snapshot only for that thread; nested snapshots apply to the parent first. Writes outside any explicit snapshot go to the global snapshot, but apply notifications for those are deferred until Snapshot.sendApplyNotifications(). On Android, the Compose runtime registers a global write observer and schedules that call on the main dispatcher, so you don't call it yourself.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val x = mutableStateOf(1)
val s = Snapshot.takeMutableSnapshot()
try {
    s.enter { x.value = 2 }          // invisible outside until apply
    check(x.value == 1)
    s.apply().check()                // publish atomically; throws on conflict
    check(x.value == 2)
} finally { s.dispose() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting dispose() for manually taken snapshots (docs warn of hard-to-diagnose memory leaks).
  • Assuming snapshots are per-composable. They are per-thread contexts for all state.
  • Assuming a write from a background thread is instantly visible to the composition; it is visible after the global snapshot advances.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why isolate composition in a snapshot? → So a recomposition pass is consistent even if background threads write meanwhile, and so failed/abandoned passes can be discarded.
  2. What if no one calls sendApplyNotifications (e.g. unit test without Compose)? → Observers like snapshotFlow never fire; Compose UI advances it for you.
  3. How is this like STM/MVCC? → Optimistic concurrency with conflict detection at apply time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "snapshot state is Compose's observable state." Senior: describes record versions, isolation, atomic apply, global snapshot advancement, and why leaked snapshots matter.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom screenshot-test helper took snapshots and never disposed them, so state objects kept stale records and memory grew across a 2,000-test suite until the CI worker OOM'd.

questions.promptHtml: Walk through how Compose knows which composables to recompose when a state changes. Where do read observers and apply observers come in?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the central mechanism question; a complete answer chains read, write, apply, invalidate, recompose in order.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "When composition runs, the Composer sets a snapshot read observer; every State.value read is recorded against the current recompose scope. When a state is written and its snapshot applied, an apply observer sends the set of changed objects to the Recomposer, which looks up scopes that read them and marks them invalid. On the next frame, the Recomposer runs a recomposition pass over only those invalid scopes."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1. Composition creates a MutableSnapshot with readObserver/writeObserver and runs content inside enter.
  2. readObserver maps state -> scope inside the composition's observations structure.
  3. A write on any thread lands in the global snapshot (or a mutable one). registerGlobalWriteObserver (installed on Android by the UI layer) notices "a state was changed" and posts a task to run Snapshot.sendApplyNotifications() on the main thread.
  4. sendApplyNotifications advances the global snapshot and calls registered apply observers with the changed set. The Recomposer's observer calls composition.recordModificationsOf(changed), which invalidates scopes that read those objects.
  5. The Recomposer awaits the next frame via MonotonicFrameClock (Choreographer on Android) and calls performRecompose on invalid compositions.
write -> global write observer -> post sendApplyNotifications
      -> apply observers(changed set) -> scope invalidation
      -> frame clock tick -> recompose invalid scopes only

Reads in layout and draw phases are tracked similarly by SnapshotStateObserver instances owned by LayoutNode/Owner; those invalidate layout or draw without recomposing (see the phases chunk).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val handle = Snapshot.registerApplyObserver { changed, _ ->
    // `changed` is the Set<Any> of StateObjects written; Recomposer does this to invalidate scopes
}
handle.dispose()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking reads in event handlers subscribe the screen; they run outside composition.
  • Thinking write triggers synchronous recomposition; it is always deferred to a frame.
  • Believing two writes cause two recompositions; they coalesce (see Q035).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. If a scope read state A in the previous run but not the latest, does it still get invalidated by A? → Observations for a scope are cleared and rebuilt each time it runs, so no.
  2. What invalidates when a state read inside derivedStateOf changes? → The derived state is itself a dependency; scopes invalidate only when its result changes.
  3. What if the state changes while composition is running? → The write goes to global; apply notifications arrive and invalidate again; the in-flight composition keeps its own consistent snapshot.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Compose tracks reads." Senior: gives the ordered pipeline, mentions the frame clock and global write observer, and that observations are rebuilt each execution.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Debugging "recomposes every frame" often ended with finding a state written inside a LaunchedEffect loop at frame rate; the pipeline above explained why each write produced a frame of work.

questions.contextHtml:
Profile screen, 1.2M DAU. Users edit their name and the bio preview below updates. After a refactor, the bio preview stops updating, but only when the user edits the status field. Code:

class ProfileForm {            // team marked it for performance
    var name: String = ""
    var status: String = ""
}

@Stable
class ProfileFormState { var name by mutableStateOf(""); var status by mutableStateOf("") }

@Composable
fun ProfileScreen() {
    val form = remember { ProfileForm() }
    var tick by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
    Column {
        TextField(form.name, { form.name = it; tick++ })
        TextField(form.status, { form.status = it })       // no tick
        Text("edits: $tick")                               // debug label added earlier
        Text("Hello ${form.name} (${form.status})")
    }
}

Symptoms: name field works (accidentally), status never updates the preview. A reviewer suggests slapping @Stable on ProfileForm to "fix recomposition".
questions.promptHtml: Explain the bug, why @Stable on ProfileForm is wrong, and the right fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add @Stable/@Immutable to the class." That promises the compiler something false.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why does name work? Is tick there deliberately? Does ProfileForm leave the composable (is it passed to children)? Will it need to survive rotation?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace ProfileForm with the already-existing ProfileFormState, which uses mutableStateOf properties.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) properties are plain vars; no read tracking; (b) tick increments incidentally invalidate the scope on name edits; (c) TextField caching.
  4. How I'd verify each: Remove the tick label and see name also stops updating. Layout Inspector recomposition count on ProfileScreen increments only on name edits.
  5. Root cause: form.name and form.status are plain field reads, so the scope subscribes to neither. The only observable state is tick, read by the debug label. Name edits bump tick, which recomposes ProfileScreen and incidentally re-reads both fields; status edits bump nothing, so the preview stays stale. The "half works" evidence is the red flag for unobserved mutable state.
  6. Fix: Use remember { ProfileFormState() } (fields backed by mutableStateOf) and delete tick. @Stable on ProfileFormState is legitimate because the contract holds: property changes notify Composition. For rotation, rememberSaveable with a listSaver.
  7. Prevention: Review rule: any @Stable class with a non-observable public var is a bug. The compiler does not verify the contract.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't use neverEqualPolicy+touch to force updates, and I wouldn't annotate to silence compiler reports.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if ProfileForm is a data class with vals and you copy() it? → That's the immutable-state pattern and is also fine; it just replaces the whole state.
  • Does @Immutable change runtime behavior? → It only changes compiler output (skipping decisions); lying produces stale UI.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared design-system module annotated an EditorState as @Stable while exposing a plain mutable selection field. The editor "mostly worked" in QA because other state invalidated the parent; in a configuration with fewer ambient updates the cursor froze.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds @Stable and calls it done.
  • Hire: Moves fields to mutableStateOf, explains unobserved reads.
  • Strong hire: Explains that @Stable is a promise not a mechanism, and spots why the original "partly works" masking.

questions.contextHtml:
Shopping app, 800k DAU, mid-range devices (Snapdragon 6-series). A collapsing toolbar was added to a product page with 40 composables. After release, scroll jank rate rises from 4% to 19% on Pixel 6a-class devices. Perfetto shows the main thread doing ~9 ms of Compose work per frame during scroll (budget 16.6 ms at 60 Hz). The code:

@Composable
fun ProductScreen(scroll: ScrollState, product: Product) {
    val offset = scroll.value                   // read in composition
    Column(Modifier.verticalScroll(scroll)) {
        Toolbar(alpha = (1f - offset / 300f).coerceIn(0f, 1f))
        Gallery(product.images)
        Details(product)
        Reviews(product.reviews)
    }
}

Red herring: someone suspects image loading; Coil traces look fine.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add remember around things" or "use derivedStateOf" without noticing the read happens in a high scope for every pixel.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is Toolbar the only consumer of the offset? Are Gallery/Details/Reviews skippable (stable params)? Does the regression correlate with the toolbar commit? Release build with baseline profile?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a flag to disable the fade (alpha fixed) while the fix lands.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) scroll.value read in the root scope recomposes the whole screen body every scroll pixel; (b) children unskippable (List params unstable), amplifying it; (c) image decode; (d) overdraw.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector recomposition counts: ProductScreen and children counting up during scroll. Compose compiler report for Details/Reviews stability. System trace for Recomposer:recompose slices per frame.
  5. Root cause: scroll.value is read in ProductScreen's scope, so each scroll pixel invalidates it, and any child with unstable params is re-run. Scroll events arrive per frame, so ~9 ms goes to composition instead of just draw.
  6. Fix: Defer the read to a later phase: Toolbar(alpha = { (1f - scroll.value / 300f).coerceIn(0f, 1f) }) and consume it inside Modifier.graphicsLayer { this.alpha = alphaProvider() } so only the draw phase observes it. Long term: make product types stable (see stability chunk).
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark scroll test with FrameTimingMetric in CI; review checklist item: "scroll/animation values are read in lambda modifiers".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't wrap in derivedStateOf here: the value changes every pixel so it doesn't reduce invalidation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the toolbar needs layout changes, not alpha? → Read in a layout modifier Modifier.layout { } or use offset { IntOffset(...) } so only layout re-runs.
  • Does graphicsLayer lambda read re-run composition? → No; it is observed in the draw/layer phase.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a retail app: moving one scroll.value read into a graphicsLayer lambda cut per-frame composition work from ~9 ms to near zero on a 7-composable header, with no change in visuals.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames image loading; random remember.
  • Hire: Spots read-in-composition and defers it into a lambda.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies, knows which phase observes the read, uses Perfetto and recomposition counts, and notes derivedStateOf doesn't help for continuously changing values.

questions.promptHtml: Is it safe to write MutableState from a background thread? What guarantees do you get, and what breaks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common production pattern (ViewModel updating state from Dispatchers.IO). Senior engineers need to know exactly where atomicity ends.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Yes, writes from any thread go to the global snapshot and are safe against memory corruption; Compose picks them up when apply notifications run on the main thread. But there's no multi-field atomicity, and x.value += 1 is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent writers lose updates. For atomic multi-state updates, I wrap them in Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot or use one immutable state object."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Writes in the global snapshot create/overwrite records under the global snapshot's lock; the global write observer schedules sendApplyNotifications. So background writes eventually invalidate readers; the UI thread isn't blocked. However:

  • Tearing: Writing a and b separately in the global snapshot lets the composition snapshot (taken when a frame starts) see a new and b old if the frame begins between writes. Docs for withMutableSnapshot state that changes are not visible to other threads until the block returns, then become visible together.
  • Lost updates: two threads doing count.value = count.value + 1 interleave.
  • Reads in background: reading state on a background thread without a snapshot reads the global snapshot; snapshotFlow is the safe way to observe.
  • Suspension: withMutableSnapshot's block must not suspend.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Atomic from the UI's perspective
Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot {
    loading.value = false
    items.value = result
}

// Lost-update fix: counter policy or atomic primitive
val hits = mutableStateOf(0, policy = counterPolicy()) // see Q033; or hold AtomicInteger + one writer

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) { state.value = x; other.value = y } and seeing a flicker frame with inconsistent data.
  • Calling delay() or any suspend function inside the withMutableSnapshot block; the docs say the block must not suspend.
  • Assuming this is "thread-confined to main" like Views (CalledFromWrongThreadException). Compose state has no such check.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you design the ViewModel? → Single immutable UiState in a StateFlow, collect with collectAsStateWithLifecycle; covered in the architecture track.
  2. When is Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot the right tool? → Existing code with several mutableStateOf fields you cannot easily collapse.
  3. What happens if two snapshots write the same state? → Conflict at apply (Q033).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "state is thread safe in Compose" or "must be on main". Senior: separates memory safety, visibility timing, atomicity and lost updates.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout screen flickered "Loading false, items empty" for one frame on slow devices because loading and items were written separately from IO; wrapping in one snapshot (later, one UiState) removed it.

questions.promptHtml: When would you call Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot or takeMutableSnapshot yourself in app or library code, and what are the hazards?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests practical depth: very few engineers use snapshot APIs directly, and the ones who do must know apply, conflict and disposal rules.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I use withMutableSnapshot to publish a group of state writes atomically, typically from a background thread or a test. It takes a mutable snapshot, runs the block, applies it on success, and throws SnapshotApplyConflictException if a conflicting write was applied meanwhile. For manual takeMutableSnapshot I must always dispose() in a finally, and I must never suspend inside enter."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the docs: withMutableSnapshot(block) = take + enter + apply + dispose semantics; changes are invisible to other threads until the block returns, then visible together and observers like snapshotFlow are notified. takeMutableSnapshot(readObserver, writeObserver) gives finer control: you decide when/if to apply(); apply() returns a SnapshotApplyResult (Success or Failure) and .check() throws on failure. Nested snapshots apply to the parent, not to global, until the parent applies. A read-only takeSnapshot() freezes a consistent view useful for reading multiple states consistently on a background thread, and Snapshot.asContextElement() lets a coroutine re-enter a snapshot after each resumption.

API Use
Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot { } atomic multi-write
Snapshot.takeSnapshot() + enter consistent read of several states
Snapshot.withoutReadObservation { } read state without subscribing (since 1.2)
Snapshot.global { } escape current snapshot

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val snap = Snapshot.takeSnapshot()
try {
    val (a, b) = snap.enter { stateA.value to stateB.value }  // consistent pair
} finally { snap.dispose() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaking undisposed snapshots: records can't be GC'd, memory grows silently.
  • Holding a snapshot across await/delay without asContextElement, so the coroutine resumes in the wrong snapshot.
  • Using it to "fix" a design that should have one immutable state object.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does apply() run observers synchronously? → Non-nested apply notifies apply observers and makes changes visible to all new non-nested snapshots (per docs for sendApplyNotifications).
  2. Difference between takeSnapshot and takeMutableSnapshot? → The former is read-only; writes throw IllegalStateException.
  3. How does Snapshot.withoutReadObservation help? → Avoids subscribing a scope to a state you only need as a one-time value.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: never touched snapshots. Senior: names the apply result, disposal, suspension prohibition and when each is justified.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A background sync updated four state objects per tick; wrapping the writes in withMutableSnapshot removed an intermittent inconsistent-frame bug without touching the UI code.

questions.promptHtml: Two snapshots modify the same state and both try to apply. What happens, and how can a merge policy help?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you understand optimistic concurrency in the snapshot model and the contract of SnapshotMutationPolicy.merge.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Snapshot isolation is optimistic: the first apply() wins. The second finds that the state's visible record changed since it branched, so it conflicts. The policy's merge(previous, current, applied) gets one chance to produce a combined value; the default returns null, so apply fails (SnapshotApplyConflictException from withMutableSnapshot, or Failure from apply()). A custom policy such as a counter, which adds deltas, can make conflicts impossible."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
At apply time the runtime compares, per state object the snapshot wrote, three records: previous (the value when the snapshot branched), current (what's now visible in the parent/global), applied (the snapshot's value). If current equals previous there is no conflict. Otherwise it asks policy.equivalent(...) and then merge. Official docs example: counterPolicy merges as current + (applied - previous), so two snapshots adding 10 and 20 to 0 yield 30 and never conflict. With a data class you can merge disjoint fields (take applied.name if current.name == previous.name, etc.).

Two consequences: neverEqualPolicy makes every concurrent write conflict (equivalent never true, merge null). And when composition's own snapshot fails to apply, Compose discards that pass and schedules a fresh composition (docs for takeMutableSnapshot), so your composition code may run more than once with only the last result kept.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun counterPolicy(): SnapshotMutationPolicy<Int> = object : SnapshotMutationPolicy<Int> {
    override fun equivalent(a: Int, b: Int) = a == b
    override fun merge(previous: Int, current: Int, applied: Int) = current + (applied - previous)
}
val total = mutableStateOf(0, counterPolicy())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming conflicts are rare so no handling is needed: with background writers and withMutableSnapshot, they appear under load.
  • Returning null from a nullable-typed policy: null means failure, ambiguous if T? is legitimate.
  • Writing a merge that isn't commutative, producing order-dependent state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does a failed withMutableSnapshot do? → Throws SnapshotApplyConflictException; none of the block's writes are applied. Retry or restructure.
  2. Can plain mutableStateOf writes conflict if both write the same value? → Not under structural equality: equal values are treated as non-conflicting.
  3. Why not just use a lock? → Compose reads are lock-free per snapshot; optimistic apply avoids blocking frames.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "I've never seen that." Senior: explains previous/current/applied, shows counterPolicy, and knows when it matters in production.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An analytics overlay counted events from two coroutines in separate snapshots; under load it threw conflict exceptions intermittently until the counter used a merging policy.

questions.contextHtml:
Orders list screen, 500k DAU. After a refactor, QA sees the device get hot on this screen; battery team flags 100% CPU on one core. Layout Inspector shows OrdersScreen recomposing about 60 times per second while idle. A senior reviewer notes no network calls. The code:

@Composable
fun OrdersScreen(orders: List<Order>) {
    val sorted = remember { mutableStateListOf<Order>() }
    var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }

    sorted.clear()
    sorted.addAll(orders.sortedByDescending { it.createdAt })   // "keep sorted copy in state"
    count = sorted.size                                         // for the header

    Column {
        Text("Orders: $count")
        sorted.forEach { OrderRow(it) }
    }
}

Red herring: the team suspects OrderRow images.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap in LaunchedEffect", without explaining why the loop exists, or "add remember(orders)" without noticing the writes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is orders a new instance each parent recomposition? What's calling OrdersScreen? Is there a warning in logcat? Which state does the idle recomposition read?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Compute val sorted = remember(orders) { orders.sortedByDescending { it.createdAt } } and drop the state writes; ship as hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) state written after being read in the same composition (backwards write); (b) parent re-sends new list each frame; (c) animation upstream; (d) image loader.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log in the body to count executions; Layout Inspector count rising with no input; comment out the writes and watch the count stop; check caller for derived list creation.
  5. Root cause: sorted.clear()/addAll and count = ... run during composition. sorted.forEach and $count read the same state objects after writing them (a backwards write: the state was modified after reads by this scope in earlier runs). Each pass writes a structurally changed list (clear then addAll always bumps the list's modification), the apply invalidates the scope that read it, so it recomposes again next frame, and again. The write also happens on every recomposition regardless of whether orders changed.
  6. Fix: Derive, don't store: val sorted = remember(orders) { orders.sortedByDescending { it.createdAt } } and Text("Orders: ${sorted.size}"). Sort in the ViewModel when the sort is a data concern. Compose docs on side effects require composables to be free of side effects; writes belong in event handlers or effects.
  7. Prevention: Lint rule/review check "state write inside a composable body"; consider Snapshot.readOnly style guard where available (added in runtime 1.14.0-alpha01; verify before relying on it). Add a test that asserts recomposition count is stable after idle.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not moving it into LaunchedEffect(orders) just to move the write: it'd cost an extra recomposition and an inconsistent first frame for derived data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the sort is expensive (50k items)? → Compute off-thread in the ViewModel or produceState; keep composition cheap.
  • Why doesn't Compose throw? → It supports writes before reads in a single pass (the write observer invalidates scopes that haven't read yet), so it can't tell this loop from intended behavior.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a media app: a "normalize list" helper executed list.sort() on a SnapshotStateList inside composition. In debug it ran at frame rate silently; the clue was a perfetto trace with Recomposer:recompose slices back-to-back.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Cannot find the loop.
  • Hire: Identifies writes in composition and derives with remember(orders).
  • Strong hire: Explains write-after-read invalidation, why the runtime doesn't crash, and the architecture fix (derive upstream).

questions.promptHtml: If I change three state variables in a row in a click handler, how many recompositions happen? What does the runtime do with writes that arrive between frames?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests the mental model that recomposition is frame-driven and batched, which underpins how you reason about "extra" recompositions and batching strategies.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "One. Writes just mark the state changed in the global snapshot and ask for an apply notification. The Recomposer invalidates the scopes and waits for the next frame callback via the MonotonicFrameClock; at that frame it recomposes all invalid scopes together in one pass. So three writes in one handler (or even several handlers within the same frame) coalesce, and each scope runs at most once per frame, with the latest values."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Write -> global write observer -> sendApplyNotifications posted to main -> apply observers invalidate scopes -> Recomposer.awaitWorkAvailable wakes -> waits for frameClock.withFrameNanos (Choreographer on Android) -> performRecompose -> applies changes -> layout and draw phases run in the same frame. A scope invalidated several times before the frame still runs once. Also, state read in an effect that writes during the same frame can cause another recomposition in the following frame, not an infinite synchronous loop.

t0 click: a=1; b=2; c=3   (3 writes, 0 recompositions yet)
t0+: apply notification -> scopes invalid
t1 vsync/frame callback -> recompose once (a,b,c all new)

Consequences: you never need manual debouncing for same-frame writes; high-frequency writers (sensors, sockets) cost at most one pass per frame but each pass still does the work of all invalid scopes (see Q039).

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Button(onClick = { a++; b++; c++ }) { Text("go") }   // one recomposition of scopes reading a/b/c

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Snapshot.sendApplyNotifications() in app code to "force" recomposition; it's unnecessary and may mask threading bugs.
  • Assuming a written value can be read back unchanged inside the same composition pass; the composition snapshot is isolated from newer global writes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can writes cause recomposition in the same frame as they occur? → Only if apply happens before the frame callback runs; the scopes still run once.
  2. Does Dispatchers.Main.immediate matter? → It changes when your code runs, not when recomposition runs.
  3. How does this interact with snapshotFlow? → snapshotFlow emits after apply, conflating intermediate values, collected on its dispatcher.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "each write recomposes." Senior: frame-clock batching and why batching writes rarely matters while heavy per-frame work does.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Engineers added a debounce around three dependent writes thinking they would cause three recompositions; deleting it simplified code and changed nothing in traces.

questions.promptHtml: What can you assume about the order, number of times and threads a composable function runs on?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The official guidance says composables must be free of order/thread assumptions. Interviewers use it to detect hidden side effects.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Nothing. Compose docs state composables may run in any order, may be skipped, may run frequently (even every frame of an animation), may be executed in parallel in the future, and recomposition can be cancelled and restarted. So composable bodies must be idempotent and side-effect free; anything with a side effect belongs in an effect handler or event callback."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Order: Siblings are normally composed top to bottom, but the runtime is free to compose invalid scopes in any order. Code that writes lateinit globals in one composable and reads them in another is broken.
  • Skipping: A child may not run at all (Q023); don't rely on it to set up something.
  • Frequency: A composable under an animation may run every frame; logging/analytics there overcounts.
  • Parallelism: The runtime is designed to allow composing on multiple threads (the Thinking in Compose page describes it as a future/possible capability; today Android composition runs on the UI thread by default; verify per release). So don't touch non-thread-safe shared objects.
  • Cancellation/abandonment: A recomposition can be discarded if snapshot apply fails or composition is cancelled; its effects (e.g. objects created in remember) get onAbandoned (Q037).
Bad:  @Composable fun Row(item) { analytics.track("viewed"); counter++ }
Good: LaunchedEffect(item.id) { analytics.track("viewed") }

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Badge(count: Int) {
    // BUG: executed an unpredictable number of times, in unpredictable order
    globalMaxBadge = maxOf(globalMaxBadge, count)
    Text("$count")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Counting impressions in composition.
  • Reading a variable mutated by a sibling composable assuming order.
  • Writing to a non-thread-safe shared map from composables.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do side effects go? → LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect, SideEffect, event handlers.
  2. Does parallel composition exist today? → Don't depend on either; verify in release notes.
  3. Does a lambda in onClick need to be idempotent? → No; it's not composition.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "no side effects in composables." Senior: enumerates the four unpredictabilities and connects them to abandonment and skipping.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "viewed" analytics count was 3x too high because impressions fired in composition and the list recomposed on scroll.

questions.promptHtml: What happens to remembered objects if a composition pass is thrown away before it is applied? How does RememberObserver relate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It probes knowledge of optimistic composition and resource lifecycle correctness for custom state holders.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Composition is optimistic: results are only committed at apply. If the pass is discarded (apply conflict, cancellation, an exception), objects created by remember during that pass never became part of the live composition. If they implement RememberObserver, Compose calls onAbandoned() instead of onRemembered(). So onRemembered is where I start resources, and onAbandoned/onForgotten is where I clean up; I must not start work in the constructor."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: RememberObserver has three callbacks: onRemembered (the object has been committed to composition), onForgotten (it left composition), onAbandoned (the composition that created it was discarded before commit). Effect handlers use this machinery: LaunchedEffect's coroutine starts in onRemembered, not when the lambda first executes, so aborted passes never leak coroutines. Likewise DisposableEffect. Custom state holders that open a sensor or subscribe in init leak or double-register when a pass is retried.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SensorHolder : RememberObserver {
    override fun onRemembered() { start() }
    override fun onForgotten() { stop() }
    override fun onAbandoned() { /* nothing started, nothing to stop */ }
}
@Composable fun rememberSensor() = remember { SensorHolder() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Starting listeners in the constructor or in the remember {} lambda.
  • Doing the same in produce-like helpers instead of using DisposableEffect.
  • Assuming onForgotten always follows onRemembered synchronously after leaving; it's after apply.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not just use DisposableEffect? → Often you should; RememberObserver is for reusable holders.
  2. Which APIs use it? → Effect handlers and rememberCoroutineScope (verify internal details).
  3. Can an object be both remembered and abandoned? → No: one or the other per instantiation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "remember keeps objects." Senior: describes commit semantic and puts side effects in onRemembered.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A location tracker holder registered in init leaked a listener on pass retries until moved to onRemembered.

questions.contextHtml: A 300k DAU travel app is migrating its search screen from LiveData to Compose. A dev proposes: "Just expose var results by mutableStateOf(emptyList<Hotel>()), var loading by mutableStateOf(false) and var error by mutableStateOf<String?>(null) directly in the ViewModel and write them from Dispatchers.IO." In a trial, 1 in ~400 sessions on low-end devices briefly shows an empty list with loading = false (flash of 'No results') before results appear. The team lead asks you to decide.
questions.promptHtml: Do you accept the proposal? What are the correctness issues and what do you recommend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "State must only be written on main" (not a Compose rule), or "use LiveData" without a reason.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the ViewModel Android-only or KMP? Do we test the ViewModel with plain JVM tests? Do other components (widgets, analytics) need the state? Who else reads these properties?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Before refactoring, wrap the three writes in Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot { ... } to remove the flash.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) tearing: loading and results are written separately into the global snapshot; a frame that starts between them sees loading=false, results=old; (b) ordering bug in the repository code; (c) race of two overlapping searches; (d) stale state restore. Frequency on slow devices points to (a).
  4. How I'd verify each: Add temporary log of the pair as read in composition; reproduce with an artificial delay between writes; Perfetto to see a frame between the IO writes; debug a concurrent search with logs on request ids.
  5. Root cause: Each mutableStateOf write is individually visible; there's no transaction across them unless you use a snapshot (Q031).
  6. Fix: Recommend a single immutable UiState(results, loading, error) in a StateFlow, updated with update {} (atomic CAS), collected via collectAsStateWithLifecycle. That gives atomic multi-field updates, JVM testing without the Compose runtime, lifecycle-aware collection, and KMP-compat. If the team insists on Compose state in the VM, then all multi-field writes must go through withMutableSnapshot and the properties must be private set.
  7. Prevention: Convention: one state object per screen; a unit test that asserts transitions emit consistent combinations.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Compose state in a VM ties it to the Compose runtime and snapshot semantics (tests need to advance the snapshot); StateFlow costs one collection and an equals on emissions. I wouldn't mix both in one screen.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Overlapping searches finish out of order? → Cancel the previous job (collectLatest/flatMapLatest) so only the latest writes.
  • Is StateFlow's update atomic with Compose's State? → Yes the flow value is atomic; Compose sees it after collection and collectAsState writes to a state on the collector.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a marketplace app: the flash-of-empty bug cost a measurable conversion dip on one device tier; the cure was not locking but making the state one immutable object.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Says only main-thread writes are allowed; no mention of tearing.
  • Hire: Identifies tearing; proposes withMutableSnapshot or single UiState.
  • Strong hire: Compares with StateFlow on testing/KMP/lifecycle, explains CAS update, handles overlapping requests.

questions.contextHtml: A trading-style dashboard (not executing trades; just displaying quotes) shows 60 instruments from a websocket delivering about 1,500 ticks per second in bursts. UI uses val prices = remember { mutableStateListOf<Quote>() } and the socket callback does prices[idx] = quote from an OkHttp thread. On mid-range phones, frame p95 is 38 ms (target 16.6 at 60 Hz), battery drain complaints, and the system trace shows the main thread saturated with Recomposer:recompose (~14 ms per frame) plus applyChanges. Each row does Text(price) and a sparkline Canvas.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you bring p95 under budget?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use derivedStateOf" or "debounce 100 ms" blindly, without understanding what scales with tick rate.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What's the product requirement for freshness (does a human need >10 updates/s per row)? How many rows visible at once? Is the sparkline derived from history? Is the list keyed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Throttle UI updates server-side-agnostic: sample the latest quote per instrument at 4–10 Hz before writing state.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-tick writes to a shared SnapshotStateList invalidate every scope that read the list, i.e. the list parent, so all 60 rows re-run when any row changes; (b) each write is a snapshot record copy under lock from the socket thread; (c) rows are unstable or unkeyed; (d) Canvas redraw cost.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector counts (all rows incrementing together), compiler report on Quote, trace applyChanges/recompose slices per frame, Macrobenchmark with a replay of the tick stream.
  5. Root cause: Frame coalescing (Q035) caps recompositions at one per frame, but each pass processes all invalidated scopes; because the observation granularity is the whole list, every tick invalidates the parent that iterates the list, and rows with unstable params re-run. 1,500 writes/s also cost record copying and lock contention on the socket thread.
  6. Fix: (1) Coalesce off-main: a conflate()d flow per instrument or periodic snapshot of the latest values (e.g. sample(100)), applied in one withMutableSnapshot. (2) Give each row its own state: class RowState(val id: String) { var quote by mutableStateOf(...) } so only the row that changed recomposes, passed down as State<Quote>/lambda (Q042). (3) Use keys; make Quote an immutable/stable type. (4) Draw-phase reads for sparkline via drawWithCache/Canvas reading state inside the draw lambda.
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark with a synthetic 2,000 ticks/s feed, alert on p95 frame time; document an update-rate budget.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Throttling shows slightly stale prices, so agree on a freshness SLA with product. I wouldn't delay() writes on the main thread or keep per-tick history in Compose state.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Product demands 'real-time' for one highlighted instrument? → Keep a separate unthrottled state for that row only.
  • Would moving to StateFlow<List<Quote>> fix it? → Not alone: every emission is a new list; conflation and per-row granularity still matter.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a 10 Hz sample plus per-row state turned a 38 ms p95 to ~12 ms on the same hardware, and the team learned to count writes per second as a first-class metric.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Reaches for generic memoization.
  • Hire: Throttles/conflates and splits state per row.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies per-frame cost, explains frame coalescing vs invalidation breadth, and uses benchmarks with replay.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review. A release (Compose runtime 1.7 era; verify exact) caused a crash cluster: androidx.compose.runtime.snapshots.SnapshotApplyConflictException: Apply failed at about 0.35% of sessions on the cart screen, mostly on 4 GB RAM devices. Stack points to a utility:

fun CartState.applyDiscounts(promo: Promo) = Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot {
    total.value = total.value - promo.amount
    appliedPromos.add(promo)
}

called from two coroutines on Dispatchers.Default: one for the user's coupon, one for loyalty points auto-applied after login. Both ran within ms of each other. Red herring: the OOM team claims low memory causes it.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the root cause, the fix options, and what you'd put in the post-incident actions.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Catch the exception and ignore it" (silently loses a discount) or "add a lock" without understanding why the snapshots conflict.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is total a plain mutableStateOf<Int>? Does it matter if both discounts apply? Is order important? Are these writes also read by composition?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Retry loop around withMutableSnapshot (bounded, e.g. 3 attempts) to stop the crash.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) two mutable snapshots branched from the same base both wrote total; the second apply found total changed and the default merge returned null; (b) memory pressure (red herring: slow devices only widen the race window); (c) bug in promo math.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with two coroutines and delay/barrier inside the snapshot; unit test with Snapshot.takeMutableSnapshot twice; check crash correlation with login-time autopromo.
  5. Root cause: Snapshot isolation is optimistic. Both snapshots read total=100, wrote 90 and 80. First applied; second found current(90) != previous(100) and applied(80) != current, merge null -> conflict (Q033). Because total has no merge policy, the sums can't be combined.
  6. Fix: Short term: bounded retry (recomputing from fresh state inside each attempt). Long term: model discounts as a list of applied promos (merged by adding to a list) and derive total; or use a merging policy for the counter; or serialize via a single-writer actor/Mutex in the ViewModel and expose immutable state.
  7. Prevention: Concurrency test: two coroutines applying promos 1,000 times asserting totals; breadcrumb logs on conflict count; crash-free dashboards segmented by exception class.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Retry hides systemic design issues if conflicts become frequent; a Mutex adds serialization latency but guarantees ordering. Swallowing the exception silently would lose money-affecting updates; I wouldn't.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not make both writers use Dispatchers.Main? → Valid single-writer design; just keep heavy work off main.
  • Would neverEqualPolicy help? → No, it makes every concurrent write conflict.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: the root cause was visible only with the coroutines interleaved; the team added a concurrency test and moved totals to derived state, removing an entire class of races.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Catch and ignore.
  • Hire: Explains snapshot optimistic conflict; adds retry or single writer.
  • Strong hire: Uses previous/current/applied, proposes derived state or a merge policy, and writes the concurrency test.

questions.subtopic: Read observation in layout and draw
questions.promptHtml: State reads in layout and draw lambdas don't recompose the screen. How does that work, and how does it differ from a read in composition?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks if you understand that "reading state" has phase-specific consequences, and that observation isn't unique to composition.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Each phase has its own snapshot read observer. Composition reads invalidate recompose scopes. Reads inside Modifier.layout, offset { }, or LayoutNode measure blocks are tracked by a SnapshotStateObserver that invalidates layout for that node. Reads inside drawBehind, graphicsLayer { } or Canvas lambdas invalidate only draw/layer. So the same state change can skip composition entirely if it's only read in later phases."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The UI layer's Owner (AndroidComposeView) holds OwnerSnapshotObserver, which wraps SnapshotStateObserver.observeReads(target, onChanged, block) for measure/layout/layer blocks. When a state read inside such a block changes, onChanged marks that node for re-measure, re-layout or re-draw (layer invalidation) and a frame is requested; no Recomposer involvement. This is why Modifier.offset { IntOffset(x.value, 0) } is cheaper than Modifier.offset(x.value.dp): the latter reads in composition and re-creates the modifier; the former reads in the layout phase.

Read site Invalidates
composable body / args recompose scope
Modifier.layout, offset {} layout of that node
graphicsLayer { }, drawBehind {} draw / layer only

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val x = remember { Animatable(0f) }
Box(Modifier.offset { IntOffset(x.value.roundToInt(), 0) }   // layout phase read
          .graphicsLayer { alpha = 1f - x.value / 500f })    // draw/layer phase read

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the parameter overload (offset(x.dp)) and wondering why the screen recomposes at 60 fps.
  • Reading .value into a local val in composition and then using it inside the lambda; the read already happened in composition.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you verify no recomposition? → Layout Inspector counts stay flat; trace shows layout/draw only.
  2. Do lambda modifiers allocate? → A new lambda per recomposition, but not per frame while state changes.
  3. Can reads in SubcomposeLayout measure blocks cause composition? → Yes, they can force subcomposition of the slots.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use lambda versions for animation." Senior: explains per-phase observers and that the lambda defers the read, not just the modifier.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The scroll-toolbar incident in Q030 was fixed purely by moving the read into graphicsLayer {}.

questions.promptHtml: When should a composable parameter be State<T> or () -> T instead of T? What does it change at runtime?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the practical application of read-scope reasoning and a common senior-level optimization question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Passing a value reads the state in the caller's scope, so every change recomposes the caller and re-calls the child with the new argument. Passing State<T> or a provider lambda defers the read into the child (or into a later phase), so only the child's scope, or just layout/draw, is invalidated. I use it for high-frequency values like scroll offsets and animations, and not for ordinary values where clarity matters more."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Reading x.value at the call site means the parent is subscribed to x. With Child(x) where x: State<Int>, the parent only reads the State reference, which never changes; Child reads x.value and subscribes itself. A lambda () -> Int works the same way (and also works for non-State sources). Trade-offs: slightly harder previews/tests, less obvious API, and lambda identity: provider lambdas capturing a State are stable only if the captured state reference is stable; with strong skipping lambdas are memoized, in classic mode wrap in remember when needed (verify per compiler version).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable fun Parent(scroll: ScrollState) {
    Header(offset = { scroll.value })     // Parent doesn't read scroll.value
}
@Composable fun Header(offset: () -> Int) {
    Box(Modifier.graphicsLayer { translationY = -offset() / 2f })  // read in draw phase
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using State<T> params everywhere; API noise with no benefit when values rarely change.
  • Reading offset() in the child's composition body; you just moved the recomposition down.
  • Exposing MutableState as a parameter, letting children write.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. State<T> vs () -> T? → Lambda is more flexible and testable; State is simpler for pure Compose.
  2. Does this change skipping? → The parent often becomes skippable; the child's scope is invalidated by the read.
  3. Is there a risk? → Hidden dependency: the child's output changes without its parameters changing, which surprises people reading the code.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: passes values everywhere. Senior: chooses based on read frequency and the phase where the read should happen.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Switching a progress indicator parameter to a provider lambda stopped a 200-row screen from recomposing during a 30 fps upload progress update.
